newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina sees cool welcome for Clinton over trade.
newsitem.headline: Argentina sees cool welcome for Clinton over trade.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton will get a cool reception when he visits Argentina in October if he stands by his punitive trade action in a row over patents, Argentine Congressmen said Wednesday.
Argentina is bristling at Clinton's decision Tuesday to withdraw trade benefits over what he called "inadequate" intellectual property protection under new Argentine laws.

"Clinton will not find it very pleasant when he visits our country," said opposition Radical Party deputy Juan Pablo Baylac, vice-president of the lower house of Congress's Industry Committee which is united against the U.S. move.
The long-running patent row with Washington, focused on the pharmaceuticals industry, strikes a nationalist chord.
Ruling Peronist Party deputies have united with Radical and Frepaso opposition deputies to demand an appeal to the World Trade Organization and fierce retaliatory measures.
They are calling it a question of sovereignty and find the government's response -- condemning the U.S. move as "unfair sanctions" but shying from retaliation -- unsatisfactory.

"We believe we should go further," said Humberto Roggero, Peronist, chairman of the Industry Committee, which wants the government to go to the World Trade Organization and exclude U.S. firms from privatizations while the "sanctions" last.

U.S. trade officials say the measures will remain in place until Argentina "takes steps to improve" its legislation. The White House says the 50 percent cut in the number of products that can be imported duty-free under the Generalized System of Preferences will affect $260 million of Argentine goods.
Argentine industry expects it to cost $20 million a year in lost exports.
President Carlos Menem's government, which first tried to get patent laws closer to what Washington wanted but saw them watered down by Congress, refuses to bow to U.S. pressure.

"Argentina will bear these measures, but the government will not modify its legislation which is completely satisfactory," said Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella Tuesday, calling the U.S. measures "unnecessary and arbitrary."

Washington takes particular exception to the five-year transition period, which it says leaves its pharmaceutical companies still open to "piracy." U.S. drug firms say they lose $500 million a year to Argentine copies.
But Argentina argues that its legislation more than meets WTO requirements and it could have had a 10-year transition.
Congress wants the government to get Argentina's partners in the Mercosur regional trade bloc -- Brazil, Uruguay and Paraguay -- to show solidarity by applying the same sanctions on U.S. companies.
"We expect the support of Mercosur countries. Only by showing solidarity can we defend the region's interests," Roggero told a news conference.

Argentina's Economy Ministry said Wednesday that it was "pretty annoyed" and considering WTO action, but turned down the call for retaliation, saying it was not helpful when the country still had recourse to forums like the WTO.
Economy Ministry Coordination Secretary Julio Caceres pledged to put the issue to U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley when he visits Argentina next month.
